source: Royal Government of Cambodia, General Directorate of Agriculture (GDA) / Boosting Food Production Program (PMO), "ខែ្សសង្វាក់ផលិតកម្ម ដំណាំពោតនៅកម្ពុជា" (Corn Production Value Chain in Cambodia), 2017
text:
The document summarizes constraints facing each type of actor in the red-corn value chain, grouped into three categories (input suppliers, producers/farmers, and collectors/exporters):

Input suppliers face: farmers not committing to buying from a particular supplier consistently (switching between suppliers depending on convenience/price); a lack of quality-certified seed specifically tailored to farmer needs; no fixed/standard quality grading for seed, fertilizer or agrochemicals, so buyers cannot verify claims before purchase; and the fact that many input dealers extend informal credit/loans to farmers and machinery-service providers without formal repayment guarantees, creating financial risk for the suppliers themselves.

Producers/farmers face: unpredictable rainfall and drought; growing dependence on wet-cob and dried-kernel corn markets that fluctuate; pest and disease pressure that they lack the technical knowledge to manage effectively; and structural risk in that the whole chain still functions on trust/relationship-based dealing rather than formal contracts, leaving farmers exposed if a buyer simply doesn't show up or offers a lower price than expected at harvest time.

Collectors/exporters face: dependence on farmer-reported information about crop volume with no independent verification; limited access to storage infrastructure; heavy reliance on informal trust-based relationships with both farmers and cross-border buyers; risk that the export market (Thailand/Vietnam) can shift price or demand suddenly, leaving Cambodian collectors exposed; being seen by some farmers as "outsiders" not from the local community, which limits trust and repeat business; and quality inconsistency in the corn they receive from many small, uncoordinated farmer suppliers.
